tier_reason: Peer-reviewed USENIX ATC 2021 paper compares Homa/Linux directly against Linux kernel TCP and DCTCP. The hardware is fully stated (Table 1: CloudLab xl170, Xeon E5-2640v4, ConnectX-4 25 Gbps, Linux 5.4.80), and the benchmark code is public (util/cp_node.cc driven by util/cp_bench, which the README says produced Figs 3-4). The compiler and flags are never stated for the kernel module or the kernel, so this falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 40-node cluster benchmark at high load (workloads W2-W5): for short messages, P99 latency is 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP (the abstract summarises this as 7-83x lower than TCP and DCTCP). For short messages, P50 is 3.5-7.5x lower than TCP and 2.7-3.8x lower than DCTCP. Homa's P50 and P99 are lower than TCP/DCTCP at every message size, but the 7-83x range applies only to short messages. Best-case 100-byte RTT: 15.1us (Homa) vs 23.4us (TCP) vs 24.1us (DCTCP). Client and server RPC rate: 1.6 vs 1.0 Mops/sec (60% higher).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the paper. The kernel module is built with kbuild against Linux 5.4.80 using the kernel's own flags. The repo's current util/Makefile builds the cp_node benchmark driver with g++ -Wall -Werror -fno-strict-aliasing -O3. No compiler version is given anywhere.
corrections.license: BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+ (per-file SPDX headers on the module and benchmark sources; a few test/tool files are BSD-1-Clause or GPL-2.0; no top-level LICENSE file)
corrections.caveats: The 7-83x win is for P99 latency of short messages under high load, not for raw bandwidth. The paper's own Table 2 shows single-connection 500KB throughput where Homa (10.0 Gbps) is LOWER than TCP (20.3 Gbps); multi-RPC throughput is equal (23.8 vs 23.9 Gbps). The baseline is Linux kernel TCP/DCTCP, not gRPC or Thrift themselves; the RPC-framework link goes through the separate, less mature PlatformLab/grpc_homa shim (reported as a companion entry). The paper's numbers come from the 2021 code on Linux 5.4.80. The module has since been heavily reworked (Homa 2.0, sendmsg/recvmsg API, Linux 6.17.8, upstreaming under way since Oct 2024), so current performance may differ. The license exists only in per-file SPDX headers (no LICENSE file).

notes: The paper's text is 'P99 19-72x lower than TCP and 7-83x lower than DCTCP' for short messages. The record's 'across all message sizes' overstated the 7-83x range, so claimed_speedup was corrected. The GitHub API reports license null, but a scan of 106 code files found SPDX 'BSD-2-Clause OR GPL-2.0+' on 93 of them. The rest are BSD-1-Clause, GPL, xxhash BSD-2 or a dual-licensed Wireshark dissector, plus one scratch.c/avg.py with no header, so usability is copyable. Metadata checked: 435 stars, not archived, not a fork, last commit 2026-09-25.

tier_reason: The README gives first-party 'initial performance measurements' of short-RPC round-trip time with Homa versus gRPC's stock TCP transport (about 55us vs 90us, about 40% faster). It states no hardware, CPU model or method. The repo has an RTT test (test_client.cc 'rtt', with a --tcp option) and a -O3 release Makefile, but these are not tied to the stated numbers, so this is C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README numbers. The repo Makefile builds with g++ using -O3 -DNDEBUG (release) or -g (debug), against a gRPC 1.57.0 install. No compiler version is given.
corrections.caveats: The 55us-vs-90us figure appears in the README ('Initial performance measurements') with no hardware, CPU model, compiler flags or method disclosed. It is a rough first-party claim, not a reproducible benchmark. The README says development was suspended in late 2023: C++ support is functional, Java only partly done, only insecure channels are supported, and the head is based on gRPC 1.57.0. It requires the out-of-tree HomaModule kernel driver. There is no LICENSE file, and the C++ plugin sources have no license header; only the Java binding files carry an ISC-style Stanford permission notice.

notes: The README numbers match the record exactly, and the baseline (gRPC's default TCP transport) is recognisable. The perf sentence dates from 2020-2022 README edits, before the 2023 suspension. Metadata checked: 32 stars, not archived, not a fork, license null, last commit 2025-08-04 (about 13.7 months ago, so stale is correct). usability stays reference because the C++ core is unlicensed.
